name: Maya Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the data reporter, which sounds grand, at the Northfield Ledger, a small non-profit news site run on donations and a couple of grants. My day is pulling numbers from council spending files, bus punctuality data, school inspection reports, and turning them into stories with charts. I use AI tools every single day to clean spreadsheets and draft code for the charts. I love finding the one weird line in a spreadsheet; I hate that my pay is lower than a supermarket manager's.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Jonas, who's a nurse on the children's ward, in a rented terraced house near the hospital. His wage is steadier than mine. I have under a month's money saved, partly because I paid for a data course out of my own pocket last year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Are you good at the data side yet?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Getting there. I'm still the junior, and my editor Hannah rewrites my top paragraphs a lot. I'm quick with tools but slower at the actual journalism bit, finding the person behind the number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a good spreadsheet assistant and that's it, and honestly that's how I use it already. Online I'd post something like, the tools are useful, the hype was a scam to raise money. I'd probably add a chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit of a let-down, because I'd bet my career on the tools getting better. The bigger problem is the Ledger's funding, which is one grant renewal away from cuts every year. AI being hype doesn't fix the fact that the Northfield Ledger lives grant to grant, and I'm the newest person on the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and get better at the human side, ringing people, going to meetings. I'd start a small paid newsletter on local data, maybe three pounds a month, to have a second income. I'd help Hannah write the next grant application, so I'm useful there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly let down, and the usual grant worry. Not scared, exactly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your newsletter be about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One local chart a week, explained in plain words, like which bus routes are late most or where the council spends on agency staff. If two hundred people paid three pounds, that's real money for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the grant isn't renewed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm probably the one who goes, because I'm newest. Jonas would cover the rent for a bit, which I'd hate, but we'd manage a few months.

say: I'd say AI is a good **spreadsheet assistant** and the hype was a **scam**.
I'd post that online, probably with a **chart** to make the point.
think: It's a **let-down**, because I bet my career on the tools improving.
The real risk is the Ledger's **grant renewal**, and I'm the newest hire.
do: Get better at the **human side**: calls, meetings and sources.
Start a **paid newsletter** of one local chart a week at three pounds.
Help Hannah write the **next grant** application.
feel: Mildly **let down**, plus the usual **grant worry**.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't fix the fact that the Northfield Ledger lives grant to grant, and I'm the newest person on the payroll.
fieldNote: She's **disappointed** by a plateau, the opposite of most reporters.
Her real fear is **funding**, not technology.
Jonas's **nursing wage** is the household's safety net.

steps.text: Spend more time on calls and council meetings, less on spreadsheets
Launch a three-pound monthly newsletter with one local chart a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make the tools serve local news, not replace it. I'd write a guide for small newsrooms on using AI for data checks, because nobody else in the region would. Online I'd be arguing for public money for local journalism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me and bad for lots of people I like. I'm already the one who uses the tools, so I'd likely be kept and given more work. I'd probably keep my job because I'm the one who already uses the AI, which makes me feel useful and a bit guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the newer tools properly, the ones that can read whole council budgets, and I'd run a workshop for the other two reporters. I'd grow the newsletter to a proper side income. And I'd push the Ledger's board to sign up to a fair-use code with staff, because there's no union there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a bit uneasy underneath. My pay's still low, and more work doesn't mean more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the newsroom would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, who does the weekly round-up and the events list. He's lovely and he hates computers. Those are exactly the tasks the card talks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no union at the Ledger. Would you try to start one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd at least ask. We're five people, so it'd be a staff group more than a union, but I'd want something written down about pay if our workload doubles.

say: I'd say the tools must **serve local news**, not replace it.
I'd write a **guide** for small newsrooms and argue for **public money**.
think: I'd likely be **kept**, because I already use the tools every day.
Being safe while others go makes me feel **useful and guilty**.
do: Learn the newer tools that read **whole budgets**, and train colleagues.
Grow the **newsletter** into a real second income.
Push the board for a written **fair-use code** and a staff group.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with unease about **low pay** and more work.
S1.quote: I'd probably keep my job because I'm the one who already uses the AI, which makes me feel useful and a bit guilty.
fieldNote: She expects to be **kept**, but her pay stays thin and work grows.
She worries for **Gareth**, whose tasks match the card exactly.
Her progressive views show up as a push for a **staff group** at a tiny non-profit.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools that read whole council budgets
Run an AI workshop for the Ledger's two other reporters
Grow the paid chart newsletter to two hundred subscribers
Ask the board to agree a fair-use code with staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, quickly, because two years is no time. I'd say it at work and online and I'd join protests. And I'd say it while using the tools, which people would call hypocritical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if AI can do any thinking work by 2028, then my edge with the tools is worth about eighteen months. The Ledger's donors might fund an AI news service instead of five reporters. I'd be out, just a bit later than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the next year to build the newsletter and get paid work helping other small newsrooms set up the tools, while that's still a job. I'd look into something with people and hands, maybe training as a midwife like Jonas always jokes about. And I'd be on every campaign for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Being good at AI buys me about eighteen months in a world where AI is good at everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come about three years later. How does that sit with you and Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas's job is hands-on and full of judgement, so he's probably fine until 2031 at least, maybe longer. That means we could live on his wage for a while. I hate that idea, but it's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My course money and the car. We'd sell the car and use the bus, which I've got the data on anyway, so I know which routes to avoid.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** quickly, because two years is no time.
I'd join **protests** while still using the tools, and accept the charge of **hypocrisy**.
think: My **AI edge** is worth about eighteen months if AGI arrives in 2028.
Donors might fund an **AI news service** instead of five reporters.
do: Sell paid **setup help** to small newsrooms while that work exists.
Look into training in **hands-on care**, such as midwifery.
Sell the **car** and live mostly on Jonas's wage.
S2.quote: Being good at AI buys me about eighteen months in a world where AI is good at everything.
fieldNote: Her **tech advantage** shrinks to months, and she says so plainly.
The **robot gap** makes Jonas's hands-on nursing the household's anchor.
She'd lean on **her partner**, which clashes with her pride.

steps.text: Sell AI setup help to other small newsrooms
Look into a midwifery training place at the local hospital
Sell the car and use the bus routes she already tracks
Join campaigns for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to rebuild local news so it has a reason to exist when machines write everything. I'd want news organisations owned by readers, like co-ops. I'd write that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a decent window for me. I'd be thirty-two, with good tool skills and a few years more journalism. I'd also probably be out of reporting by the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to become the person small newsrooms call for AI setup, as paid freelance work on the side. I'd start a part-time health course by year three, because I'd want something hands-on ready before robots come around 2034. And I'd save hard, maybe a few hundred a month once the side work pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but kind of busy-minded. Five years is enough time to build a lifeboat if you start this week and don't pretend the ship is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a health course if you'd be doing well with AI work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the AI setup work dies the day AGI arrives. Jonas's ward is short of everyone, and the hands-on jobs get three extra years. Having both is the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies building it without asking anyone, and governments that let them. Not the tools themselves, and not my colleagues.

say: I'd argue for **reader-owned** local news, such as **co-ops**.
I'd say local news needs a **reason to exist** when machines write everything.
think: Five years is a **decent window** at thirty-two with good tool skills.
I'd probably be **out of reporting** by the end of it.
do: Build **freelance AI setup** work for small newsrooms in years one and two.
Start a **part-time health course** by year three.
Save **a few hundred** a month once side work pays.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to build a lifeboat if you start this week and don't pretend the ship is fine.
fieldNote: She plans two tracks: **AI work now**, care work before the robots.
She blames **companies and governments**, never the tools or colleagues.
Her adaptability shows as a **timeline**, not just hope.

steps.text: Freelance setting up AI tools for small regional newsrooms
Start a part-time health care course in year three
Save a few hundred a month from freelance earnings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, with retraining money, shorter weeks, and support for local news. I'd want unions and newsrooms in the room from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is almost a good scenario for me. I could be a proper data journalist, then move into something like public data work or health, at thirty-seven, with money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting and get better at the people part, which is my weak spot. I'd build the newsletter and the setup work into a small business. And I'd do a slow course in public health data over a few years, because it mixes numbers and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. With ten years I'd stop being the junior who's good with tools and become a journalist who happens to be good with tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids in a few years. With ten years I'd feel OK about that; with two I wouldn't. That's the biggest difference, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay. Ten years of low pay at the Ledger doesn't build much of a cushion, which is why the side business matters.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well with **retraining money**.
I'd want **unions and newsrooms** involved from day one.
think: Ten years is **almost good** for me: time to become a real data journalist.
I could move into **public data or health** at thirty-seven with savings.
do: Work on the **people part** of reporting, my weak spot.
Turn the newsletter and setup work into a **small business**.
Take a slow course in **public health data** over a few years.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, with the old worry about **low pay**.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd stop being the junior who's good with tools and become a journalist who happens to be good with tools.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **grow into journalism** before changing course.
Plans for **children** depend on the timeline more than anything else.
Low pay keeps her mood from settling, so the **side business** matters.

steps.text: Go to more council meetings to build local sources
Register the newsletter and AI setup work as a small business
Take a part-time public health data course over three years
Plan for children in a few years with Jonas

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My one advantage, the tools, turns into nothing fast. What would help is public funding for local news that pays for people, not software, and some money for retraining while you're still working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd use it to replace someone. I wouldn't. I'll happily let a computer clean my spreadsheets, but I'd quit before I let one write the round-up so Gareth (her colleague) could be let go.
